lessons.title: Lab: Layout of a thermal power plant and the Rankine cycle

scenes.text: A 500 MW unit burns coal in a furnace, raises steam, spins a turbine and returns condensed water to the boiler.
Ananya traces the four circuits: coal and ash, air and flue gas, feed water and steam, cooling water.

steps.title: Four circuits
steps.body: 1. **Coal and ash:** bunker → mill → furnace → bottom ash/fly ash. 2. **Air and flue gas:** FD fan → air pre-heater → furnace → economiser → ESP → ID fan → chimney. 3. **Feed water and steam:** condenser → condensate pump → low-pressure heaters → deaerator → boiler feed pump → HP heaters → economiser → drum → superheater → turbine → condenser. 4. **Cooling water:** cooling tower or river → condenser.

steps.title: Ideal Rankine cycle
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic expansion in the turbine; 2→3 constant-pressure condensation to saturated liquid; 3→4 isentropic pump work w_p = v_f(p_boiler − p_cond); 4→1 constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler and superheater.
w_T = h₁ − h₂, w_net = w_T − w_p, q_in = h₁ − h₄, **η = w_net/q_in**. Steam rate = 3600/w_net kg/kWh; heat rate = 3600/η kJ/kWh. Efficiency rises with higher boiler pressure/temperature and lower condenser pressure; wetness at turbine exit (x > 0.88) limits expansion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring pump work (small but not zero) or using the wrong specific volume.
- Using x₂ from the wrong entropy — entropy is conserved only in the *ideal* turbine.
- Mixing kPa and MPa in v ΔP.

story.title: Why a second trip to the boiler

scenes.text: Rahul sees a tower-shaped boiler with two sets of superheater coils and asks why steam returns to the boiler midway.
Reheating keeps the steam dry in the last turbine stages and raises efficiency.

steps.title: Superheat and reheat
steps.body: **Superheating** raises mean heat-addition temperature and lowers wetness. **Reheat:** after expansion in the HP turbine, steam goes back to the boiler reheater at a lower pressure and is heated (often to the same temperature), then expands in IP/LP turbines. Typical reheat pressure ≈ 15–25 % of the boiler pressure. Benefits: moisture in the last stage reduced and efficiency up by ~4–5 %. Cost: more tubes, piping and controls.

steps.title: Quick rule
steps.body: Reheat helps most when the reheat pressure is roughly ¼ of the boiler pressure or lower; very high reheat pressure gives little gain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the first heat-addition term in q_in (reheat heat must be added).
- Forgetting to include HP *and* LP turbine work.
- Assuming reheat always gives huge gains: it gives a few points.

story.title: Stealing steam to warm the water

scenes.text: The deaerator at the plant is fed steam bled from the turbine to heat the boiler feed water.
Divya wants to know how much steam can be bled without losing work.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Feed water enters the boiler at a temperature closer to the saturation temperature, reducing the *irreversibility* in the boiler and raising the mean heat addition temperature. **Open (direct-contact) heaters** mix bled steam with feed water — the deaerator removes dissolved O₂ and CO₂. **Closed heaters** use shell-and-tube exchangers with drains cascaded back. Modern units: 7–8 heaters (3 LP + deaerator + 3 HP).

steps.title: Bleed fraction
steps.body: Open heater energy balance: y h_bleed + (1 − y) h_pump = h_f(heater) → **y = (h_f − h_cond)/(h_bleed − h_cond)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the whole flow in the LP turbine (only 1−y passes there).
- Using h of the condensate at the wrong point for q_in: after the heater, feed water is saturated liquid at heater pressure (plus pump).
- Forgetting that multiple heaters give more efficiency, with diminishing returns.

lessons.title: Cogeneration, supercritical cycles and plant performance indices

scenes.text: A sugar mill in Maharashtra burns bagasse to generate electricity and uses exhaust steam to boil cane juice.
This is cogeneration — high fuel utilisation.

steps.title: Cogeneration (CHP)
steps.body: Back-pressure turbines exhaust at the process steam pressure; pass-out (extraction) turbines supply steam at an intermediate pressure. **Energy utilisation factor** = (W + Q_process)/Q_fuel — can reach 70–85 %. Used in sugar, paper, fertiliser and refinery industries.

steps.title: Supercritical and ultra-supercritical
steps.body: Above the critical point (22.06 MPa, 374 °C) there is no boiling: once-through boilers. Supercritical units operate near 24 MPa/565 °C and ultra-supercritical above 25–28 MPa/600 °C+, giving net efficiencies ≈ 40–45 % vs 33–38 % for subcritical, cutting coal use and CO₂ per kWh. India's newer large units (660/800 MW) are supercritical.

steps.title: Solved example · Utilisation factor
steps.body:
A back-pressure turbine produces 5 MW of electricity and supplies 20 MW of process heat from a boiler using 30 MW of fuel: energy utilisation = (5 + 20)/30 = **83.3 %**; electrical efficiency only 5/30 = 16.7 %.
Heat rate of a station with η = 38 %: 3600/0.38 = **9474 kJ/kWh**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing a CHP's total efficiency with a power-only plant's electrical efficiency.
- Believing supercritical steam boils: it undergoes a continuous change in properties.
- Expressing heat rate in kJ/kWh and efficiency in % interchangeably without 3600.

lessons.title: Lab: Coal, combustion and boiler efficiency

scenes.text: A power station receives a rake of washed coal; the chemist reports proximate and ultimate analysis.
Faisal must estimate calorific value and boiler efficiency from the data.

steps.title: Coal analysis
steps.body: **Proximate analysis:** moisture, volatile matter, fixed carbon, ash (as received). **Ultimate analysis:** C, H, O, N, S, ash by mass. Indian thermal coals are high in ash (30–45 %) with GCV of about 3000–5500 kcal/kg, which is why large ash-handling systems are needed. **Dulong's formula:** HCV = 33 800 C + 144 000 (H − O/8) + 9270 S kJ/kg (fractions). LCV = HCV − 2442 × (9H + M).

steps.title: Boiler types and performance
steps.body:
**Fire-tube** (Lancashire, Cochran, locomotive — small, low pressure) vs **water-tube** (Babcock & Wilcox, Stirling, La Mont, Benson; high pressure, large capacity). Mountings: safety valves, water-level gauge, pressure gauge, stop valve, blow-down cock, fusible plug. Accessories: economiser, superheater, air pre-heater, feed pump, injector.
**Boiler efficiency** η = m_s (h_s − h_fw)/(m_f × CV). **Equivalent evaporation from and at 100 °C** = m_s(h_s − h_fw)/2257 (latent heat of steam at 1 atm = 2257 kJ/kg).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Dulong
steps.body: C = 0.75, H = 0.05, O = 0.08, S = 0.01: HCV = 25 350 + 144 000 × (0.05 − 0.01) + 92.7 = 25 350 + 5760 + 92.7 = **31 203 kJ/kg** (for ash-free dry coal; real run-of-mine coal is much lower after ash and moisture).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Boiler efficiency
steps.body:
Steam 10 000 kg/h at h_s = 2800 kJ/kg; feed water h_fw = 420 kJ/kg; coal 1500 kg/h, CV 25 000 kJ/kg.
- Heat to steam = 10 000 × 2380 = 23.8 × 10⁶ kJ/h
- Heat in fuel = 37.5 × 10⁶ kJ/h → **η = 63.5 %**
- Equivalent evaporation = 23.8 × 10⁶/2257 = **10 545 kg/h**; factor of evaporation = 2380/2257 = 1.054.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using HCV when the problem gives LCV (and vice versa).
- Forgetting that O is subtracted as O/8 in the Dulong formula.
- Confusing equivalent evaporation (kg/h) with factor of evaporation (a ratio).

lessons.title: Lab: Draught systems and chimney height

story.title: Why the chimney is 275 m tall

scenes.text: A new thermal plant has a very tall chimney; Gita learns the height is chosen for dispersion, not for draught.
Natural draught alone is weak, so fans do the real work.

steps.title: Draught
steps.body: The pressure difference that moves air and flue gas through the furnace. **Natural draught:** from the density difference between ambient air and hot gas column: ΔP = H g (ρ_a − ρ_g). **Mechanical draught:** forced (FD fan before the furnace), induced (ID fan after), and balanced (both; modern plants keep the furnace slightly below atmospheric, ≈ −5 mm wg). Chimney height of 220 m+ is mandated for large units to disperse SO₂ and fly ash.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Fan power
steps.body: ID fan: flow 50 m³/s, head 3 kPa, fan efficiency 0.75: P = 50 × 3000/0.75 = **200 kW**. A natural-draught chimney could never supply this head, hence mechanical draught.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gauge temperature in °C in the gas law (use kelvin).
- Forgetting that the draught depends on H, not the diameter.
- Thinking taller chimneys remove pollutants — they only dilute and disperse them.

lessons.title: Lab: Steam nozzles and impulse turbines

story.title: The jet that spins a wheel

scenes.text: De Laval's turbine spins a wheel with a high-velocity steam jet.
Imran draws the velocity triangle to find the work per kg of steam.

steps.title: Nozzle flow
steps.body: Steam expands in a convergent–divergent nozzle to convert enthalpy into kinetic energy: V = √(2(h₁ − h₂)) (V in m/s with h in J/kg) or 44.72√(Δh in kJ/kg). The **critical pressure ratio** at the throat is ≈ 0.546 for superheated steam (n = 1.3) and ≈ 0.577 for dry saturated steam (n = 1.135). Maximum discharge occurs at the throat when the critical ratio is reached (choked flow).

steps.title: Impulse turbine and velocity diagram
steps.body: Steam is expanded fully in the nozzle; the moving blades just change the direction of the jet (pressure constant across the blades). Inlet triangle: V₁ (absolute), u (blade speed), V_r1 (relative), nozzle angle α. Force = ṁ(V_w1 + V_w2); **work = u (V_w1 + V_w2)**; blade efficiency η_b = 2u(V_w1 + V_w2)/V₁². For symmetrical blades and no friction: η_b,max = cos²α at u/V₁ = ½ cos α. **Compounding** (velocity — Curtis; pressure — Rateau) reduces rotor speed.

steps.title: Solved example · Single-stage impulse
steps.body:
V₁ = 600 m/s, α = 20°, u = 250 m/s, symmetrical blades, no friction.
- V_w1 = 600 cos 20° = 563.8 m/s
- V_r,w1 = 563.8 − 250 = 313.8 m/s; for symmetrical blades the relative whirl reverses: V_r,w2 = −313.8, so V_w2 = −313.8 + 250 = −63.8 (opposite to blade motion)
- ΔV_w = 2 × 313.8 = **627.6 m/s**
- Work = 250 × 627.6 = **156.9 kJ/kg**; η_b = 156.9/(600²/2/1000) = 156.9/180 = **87.2 %**
- Maximum possible cos² 20° = 88.3 % at u = 281.9 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking ΔV_w as V_w1 − V_w2 without checking the sign of V_w2.
- Using u/V₁ = cos α instead of ½ cos α for the optimum.
- Applying critical pressure ratio 0.528 (that is for air/γ = 1.4).

lessons.title: Lab: Reaction turbines, degree of reaction and governing

scenes.text: A large power turbine has hundreds of rows of blades, each dropping pressure slightly.
Soumya studies the 50 % reaction stage.

steps.title: Reaction turbine
steps.body: Pressure drops in both fixed and moving blades; the moving blades act as nozzles and develop reaction force. **Degree of reaction** R = enthalpy drop in moving blades/total stage enthalpy drop. The **Parsons turbine** is 50 % reaction: symmetrical fixed and moving blades. Maximum efficiency η_max = 2cos²α/(1 + cos²α) at u/V₁ = cos α.

steps.title: Practical aspects
steps.body:
- **Losses:** friction, leakage, windage, exhaust (leaving) loss, mechanical.
- **Governing:** throttle (quantity of steam throttled), nozzle control (number of nozzles open), by-pass governing. Overspeed trip at ≈ 110 % speed protects the machine.
- **Reheat factor** > 1 (≈ 1.03–1.06) because multistage turbine stage efficiencies add to give a better overall than the sum of isentropic.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: 50 % reaction stage with α = 20°: cos² 20° = 0.883; η_max = 2 × 0.883/(1.883) = **93.8 %**; compare with an impulse stage's cos² α = 88.3 %. Hence reaction blading is more efficient but needs many stages and good sealing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the impulse optimum u/V₁ = ½ cos α for a Parsons stage (it is cos α).
- Forgetting axial thrust in reaction turbines (needs a balance piston).
- Confusing throttle governing's low part-load efficiency with nozzle governing's better one.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — condensers, cooling towers and cooling-water sizing

scenes.text: Nearly two-thirds of the fuel energy in a thermal plant leaves via the condenser.
Isha must size the cooling-water flow for a 210 MW unit.

steps.title: Condensers
steps.body: **Surface condenser** (shell-and-tube; steam outside, cooling water in tubes) keeps the condensate pure and holds a vacuum of ≈ 0.07–0.1 bar abs. **Jet (direct-contact) condenser** mixes steam with water (rare). Air in-leakage is removed by steam-jet ejectors or vacuum pumps. Condenser efficiency = (T_cw,out − T_cw,in)/(T_sat − T_cw,in). **Cooling towers** (natural draught hyperbolic or induced draught) evaporate part of the water to cool the rest to near wet-bulb temperature (approach 4–6 °C, range 8–12 °C); make-up water ≈ 1–2 % of circulation.

steps.title: Solved example · Cooling water
steps.body:
Steam flow 50 kg/s enters condenser with h = 2300 kJ/kg (wet), leaves as condensate h = 190 kJ/kg. Cooling water rises 10 K.
- Q = 50 × (2300 − 190) = **105 500 kW**
- ṁ_cw = 105 500/(4.18 × 10) = **2524 kg/s** (≈ 9087 m³/h)
- Cooling ratio = 2524/50 ≈ **50 kg water per kg steam**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the latent heat only, ignoring wetness.
- Confusing cooling-tower range and approach.
- Forgetting make-up water for evaporation, drift and blowdown.

lessons.title: Lab: The Brayton cycle for gas-turbine power plants

story.title: A peaker that starts in ten minutes

scenes.text: A gas-turbine station in Gujarat can reach full load in minutes to cover evening peaks.
Nikhil analyses the ideal Brayton cycle.

steps.title: Cycle and equations
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic compression (pressure ratio r_p = p₂/p₁); 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition in the combustor; 3→4 isentropic expansion in the turbine; 4→1 heat rejection to the atmosphere (open cycle).
**η_Brayton = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ)**, independent of turbine inlet temperature T₃. **Back-work ratio** = w_c/w_t ≈ 40–60 % (very high compared with steam plants, where pump work is < 1 %). Specific work is maximum for r_p,opt = (T₃/T₁)^(γ/(2(γ−1))).

steps.title: Real cycle
steps.body: With isentropic efficiencies η_c ≈ 0.85–0.88, η_t ≈ 0.88–0.92 the thermal efficiency of simple-cycle machines falls to 30–40 %. Compressor and turbine pressure losses and variable cp reduce it further. Modern heavy-duty frames use T₃ above 1400 °C with blade cooling and thermal-barrier coatings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using γ rather than (γ−1)/γ as the exponent.
- Thinking higher T₃ raises *ideal* Brayton efficiency (it does not; it raises specific work).
- Ignoring that the compressor consumes about half of the turbine work.

lessons.title: Lab: Regeneration, intercooling and combined-cycle power plants

story.title: Waste heat from a jet-engine-like exhaust

scenes.text: A gas turbine exhausts at 550 °C, hot enough to raise steam in a heat-recovery steam generator (HRSG).
Pritam adds a steam turbine to the cycle.

steps.title: Improvements
steps.body:
- **Regeneration:** exhaust heats the compressed air; works when T₄ > T₂ (low r_p).
- **Intercooling** (multistage compression) lowers compressor work: optimum interstage pressure p_i = √(p₁ p₃) for two stages.
- **Reheating** between turbine stages raises turbine work.
But each adds complexity; combined cycles are better in large plants.

steps.title: Combined cycle (CCGT)
steps.body: Gas turbine (topping, Brayton) + HRSG + steam turbine (bottoming, Rankine). **η_cc = η_g + (1 − η_g)η_s·η_HRSG** (with HRSG effectiveness folded in). Efficiencies of 55–62 % (LHV) are achieved; plant start-up is fast, capital cost low, emissions per kWh modest (natural gas). Constraint in India: limited domestic gas supply, so many CCGTs run below capacity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
η_g = 35 %, bottoming steam cycle η_s = 30 % on the gas-turbine exhaust energy: η_cc = 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.30 = **54.5 %**.
Two-stage intercooled compression from 1 bar to 16 bar: optimum interstage pressure = √(1 × 16) = **4 bar**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding η_g + η_s directly (the bottoming cycle works only on the remaining 65 %).
- Applying regeneration at high pressure ratio, where T₂ > T₄ and it would *cool* the exhaust.
- Forgetting HRSG stack losses.

lessons.title: Lab: Diesel power plants and sizing a standby generator set

scenes.text: During a grid failure, a hospital's 1 MW diesel generator starts and takes over within seconds.
The facility engineer plans fuel storage for 48 hours at 75 % load.

steps.title: Diesel power plant
steps.body: Components: diesel engine, alternator, fuel storage and day tank with filters and pumps, air intake and filtration, turbocharger, exhaust silencer, cooling system, lubrication, starting system (battery/compressed air), governor and AVR, control panel. **Uses:** standby/emergency, peak load, remote areas, isolated grids. **Advantages:** quick start, high part-load efficiency, simple. **Disadvantages:** high fuel/running cost, noise, emissions, limited unit size (up to ~20–60 MW for large low-speed engines).

steps.title: Solved example · Fuel for 48 h
steps.body:
1 MW set at 75 % load (750 kW) with bsfc = 0.21 kg/kWh: fuel = 750 × 0.21 = **157.5 kg/h**; in 48 h = 7560 kg = 7560/0.83 = **9108 litres** (diesel density 0.83 kg/L).
Overall efficiency: 3600/(0.21 × 43 000) = **39.9 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sizing fuel storage for rated rather than actual load (or vice versa) without a margin.
- Ignoring altitude and temperature de-rating (≈ 1 % per 100 m over 150 m, and ≈ 1 % per 5 °C above 40 °C — manufacturers' tables apply).
- Running gensets at very low load, which causes wet stacking.

lessons.title: Lab: Nuclear power — fission energy and reactor types

scenes.text: India operates pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWR) fuelled by natural uranium and also light-water reactors such as the VVER units at Kudankulam.
Farah wants to know how much uranium really fissions.

steps.title: Fission and reactor components
steps.body: One U-235 fission releases ≈ 200 MeV (about 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J). Components: **fuel** (UO₂ pellets in zircaloy tubes), **moderator** (slows neutrons: light water, heavy water, graphite), **control rods** (B, Cd, Hf absorb neutrons), **coolant** (water, heavy water, CO₂, liquid metal), **reflector**, **pressure vessel/pressure tubes**, **containment**. Criticality when k_eff = 1.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **PWR** (pressurised water, ~15 MPa, steam generator separate), **BWR** (boiling in the core), **PHWR/CANDU** (heavy water, natural uranium, on-power refuelling — bulk of India's fleet), **FBR** (fast breeder, liquid sodium, converts U-238 to Pu-239; India's PFBR is at Kalpakkam), **HTGR**. India's three-stage programme: PHWR → fast breeders → thorium-based reactors.

steps.title: Safety and waste
steps.body: Defence in depth: multiple barriers (fuel matrix, cladding, primary circuit, containment); emergency core cooling; passive safety. steps.title: Layout and classification
steps.body: Reservoir/dam → intake → **penstock** → surge tank (damps water hammer) → turbine → draft tube → tailrace. **Run-of-river** (no storage), **storage**, **pumped-storage** (reversible pump-turbine: pumps up in off-peak time, generates at peak — also grid balancing). By head: high (> 200 m, Pelton), medium (30–200 m, Francis), low (< 30 m, Kaplan/propeller). Hydrograph and flow-duration curves guide sizing; load-following capability is excellent.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: **P = η ρ g Q H** (W) with ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Overall efficiency η = η_penstock × η_turbine × η_generator (≈ 0.85–0.92).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Pumped storage
steps.body: A pumped-storage plant uses 100 MWh to pump (pumping efficiency 0.88) and generates with 0.90 efficiency: round-trip = 0.88 × 0.90 = **79 %**; delivered = 79.2 MWh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ρ = 1 instead of 1000 (units!).
- Using gross head when net head (after friction losses) should be used.
- Treating pumped storage as a generating source — it is storage with ~ 20 % loss.

lessons.title: Lab: Pelton, Francis and Kaplan turbines

scenes.text: A Himalayan micro-hydro site has 400 m head and small flow; a Kerala dam has 60 m; a run-of-river plant on the Ganga has 12 m.
Zoya picks a turbine for each.

steps.title: Turbines
steps.body:
- **Pelton (impulse):** high head, low flow; jets strike buckets; operated at atmospheric pressure; speed regulated by spear valve and deflector.
- **Francis (reaction, mixed flow):** medium head; spiral casing, guide vanes, runner, draft tube.
- **Kaplan (axial reaction):** low head, large flow; adjustable runner blades and guide vanes give good part-load efficiency.
**Specific speed** N_s = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in kW, H in m) classifies them: Pelton 10–35 (single jet), Francis 60–300, Kaplan 300–1000.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pelton jet
steps.body: H = 400 m, nozzle coefficient C_v = 0.98: V₁ = C_v√(2gH) = 0.98 × √(2 × 9.81 × 400) = 0.98 × 88.59 = **86.8 m/s**. Optimum bucket speed u ≈ 0.45 V₁ = **39 m/s**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Runner speed
steps.body: Jet 86.8 m/s, u = 39.1 m/s, mean bucket diameter D = 1.5 m: N = 60u/(πD) = 60 × 39.1/(π × 1.5) = **498 rpm**; in practice the generator synchronous speed (e.g. 500 rpm for 12 pole pairs at 50 Hz: N = 120 f/p = 6000/12) fixes the speed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total head for Francis when the draft tube suction head also matters.
- Ignoring cavitation: keep net positive suction head above the limit (Thoma number).
- Using synchronous-speed formula N = 120f/p with p as pole pairs (p is the number of *poles*).

steps.title: Wind power
steps.body: Kinetic energy flux through the rotor area A: **P_wind = ½ ρ A v³**. The rotor extracts a fraction C_p, limited by the **Betz limit** (16/27 = 59.3 %): P = ½ ρ A v³ C_p. Typical C_p ≈ 0.35–0.45. Power curve: cut-in speed (≈ 3–4 m/s), rated speed (≈ 11–13 m/s), cut-out (≈ 25 m/s). **Tip-speed ratio** λ = ωR/v. Types: HAWT (3-blade, dominant), VAWT (Darrieus, Savonius). Components: rotor, hub, pitch system, gearbox (or direct drive), generator (DFIG, PMSG), yaw system, tower, transformer.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Capacity factor
steps.body: A 2 MW turbine produces 5256 MWh in a year: CF = 5256/(2 × 8760) = **30 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using v² instead of v³.
- Treating the Betz limit as an engineering inefficiency (it is a physical limit).
- Ignoring air density change with altitude/temperature.

steps.title: Solar
steps.body: **PV:** a p-n junction converts photons to current; module efficiency 18–22 %; output ∝ irradiance, decreasing ≈ 0.35–0.45 %/°C with temperature. steps.title: Others

Intermittent sources need storage, forecasting and a flexible grid.

lessons.title: Lab: Load curves and load factors

story.title: A day in the grid control room

scenes.text: The state load dispatch centre watches demand climb from 3 am to an evening peak at 7 pm.
Meena converts the curve to load and capacity factors.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Connected load, maximum demand, demand factor** = max demand/connected load (< 1).
- **Load factor** = average load/peak load = energy/(peak × hours).
- **Diversity factor** = Σ individual maximum demands/coincident maximum demand (≥ 1).
- **Plant capacity factor** = actual energy/(installed capacity × hours).
- **Plant use (utilisation) factor** = actual energy/(capacity × hours of operation).
- **Reserve capacity** = installed − peak.
The **load-duration curve** orders hourly loads from highest to lowest; area = energy. Base load is the area under the minimum load; peak is the top slice.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Peak 100 MW, annual energy 438 GWh: average = 438 000 MWh/8760 = **50 MW** → LF = **50 %**. With installed capacity 150 MW: capacity factor = 438 000/(150 × 8760) = **33.3 %**; reserve = 50 MW.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Diversity
steps.body: Five feeders have individual maximum demands 120, 80, 100, 60, 140 MW (sum 500 MW); the coincident maximum is 400 MW: diversity factor = **1.25**. Higher diversity means less generating capacity per consumer served.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the load factor (relative to *peak*) with capacity factor (relative to *installed* capacity).
- Using 8760 h for a plant that ran 8000 h (use factor vs capacity factor).
- Expecting a diversity factor below 1.

lessons.title: Lab: Cost of generation, tariffs and plant selection

scenes.text: A utility compares coal, hydro and gas plants for base and peak duty.
Harpreet must compute cost per kWh and a consumer bill.

steps.title: Cost components
steps.body: **Fixed cost:** interest, depreciation, insurance, staff — independent of units generated. **Running (variable) cost:** fuel, water, consumables. **Cost per kWh = fixed cost/kWh + running cost/kWh**; fixed cost per kWh falls with a higher load factor. Coal: moderate capital, cheap fuel (base load). Gas CCGT: lower capital, expensive fuel (intermediate/peak). Hydro: high capital, near-zero fuel (peak and base). Nuclear: highest capital, low fuel (base). Diesel/gas peakers: low capital, high fuel (peak).

steps.title: Tariffs
steps.body: **Flat rate**, **block rate**, **two-part tariff** (₹/kW of max demand + ₹/kWh), **maximum demand tariff**, **time-of-day (ToD) tariff** encouraging off-peak use, power-factor clause. India's electricity is regulated by State Electricity Regulatory Commissions under the Electricity Act, 2003.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cost per kWh
steps.body: Annual fixed cost ₹120 crore (1.2 × 10⁹ ₹); 100 MW at LF 60 %: energy = 100 000 kW × 8760 × 0.6 = 525.6 × 10⁶ kWh. Fixed = 1.2 × 10⁹/525.6 × 10⁶ = **₹2.28/kWh**; fuel ₹3.00/kWh → **₹5.28/kWh**. At LF 80 %: energy 700.8 × 10⁶ kWh; fixed ₹1.71 → total ₹4.71/kWh.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Two-part bill
steps.body: Demand charge ₹200/kW/month; energy charge ₹5/kWh; maximum demand 100 kW, consumption 30 000 kWh: bill = 100 × 200 + 30 000 × 5 = 20 000 + 150 000 = **₹1,70,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spreading fixed cost over rated rather than actual output.
- Forgetting that a lower load factor raises the cost per unit.
- Confusing crore (10⁷) and lakh (10⁵).

scenes.text: Thermal plants in India must install ESPs to capture fly ash, FGD to reduce SO₂, and NOx controls under rules notified by the environment ministry.

steps.title: Pollutants and controls
steps.body:
- **Fly ash:** cyclones, **electrostatic precipitators (ESP)** (collection efficiency 99.9 %+), fabric filters (bag houses). Ash is used in cement and bricks.
- **SO₂:** low-sulphur fuel, **wet limestone FGD** (CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃/gypsum), dry sorbent injection.
- **NOx:** low-NOx burners, staged combustion, flue-gas recirculation, SCR with ammonia/urea.
- **CO₂:** efficiency improvement, carbon capture (emerging), switching fuels.
- **Thermal pollution:** closed-cycle cooling towers; **ash handling:** wet slurry or dry, ash ponds/ash mounds.

steps.title: ESP principle
steps.body: Corona discharge charges particles; the electric field drives them to collecting plates, which are rapped to drop the dust into hoppers. **Deutsch–Anderson equation:** η = 1 − exp(−w A/Q), where w is the migration (drift) velocity, A the collecting area, Q the gas flow. High-resistivity ash (low-sulphur Indian coal) makes ESPs larger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the percentage formula without the exponential.
- Ignoring that higher gas flow reduces collection efficiency.
- Treating FGD gypsum as a pure waste: it is saleable if of good quality.

steps.title: Duty and plant selection
steps.body: **Base load:** nuclear, large coal, large hydro run-of-river. **Intermediate:** CCGT, flexible coal. **Peak:** pumped storage, gas peakers, hydro with storage, diesel, batteries. Factors for site selection: fuel and water availability, load centre proximity, transport, ash disposal, environment, seismicity, land and cost.

steps.title: Grid operation
steps.body: Interconnection pools reserve capacity, improves reliability and allows economic dispatch (merit-order). Grid frequency (50 Hz nominal) reflects the balance between generation and load: low frequency means load > generation. Governors provide primary response, AGC secondary, and reserves tertiary. Variable renewables raise the need for flexibility: ramping thermal units, storage, demand response and forecasting.

steps.title: Core formulae
steps.body:
- Rankine: η = (w_T − w_p)/(h₁ − h₄); w_p = v_f Δp; steam rate = 3600/w_net; heat rate = 3600/η
- Open FWH: y = (h_f − h_c)/(h_b − h_c)
- Boiler: η = m_s(h_s − h_fw)/(m_f CV); equivalent evaporation = m_s(h_s − h_fw)/2257
- Draught: ΔP = H g (ρ_a − ρ_g)
- Impulse stage: work = u ΔV_w; η_b,max = cos²α
- Brayton: η = 1 − r_p^(−(γ−1)/γ); η_cc = η_g + (1 − η_g)η_s
- Hydro: P = ηρgQH; Wind: P = ½ρAv³C_p
- Load factor = avg/peak; capacity factor = energy/(capacity × hours)
- ESP: η = 1 − exp(−wA/Q)
- Fission: 200 MeV ≈ 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J

steps.title: Traps
steps.body: Pump work forgotten; reheat heat omitted from q_in; (γ−1)/γ vs γ; ρ = 1 in hydro formula; peak vs installed capacity; 8760 vs hours operated.

lessons.title: Lab: Steam turbine Willans line and plant visit report

scenes.text: A small back-pressure turbine drives a generator; the lab records steam flow at different loads.
The data fit a straight line — the Willans line.

steps.title: Observations
steps.body: P = 20 kW → 500 kg/h; P = 40 kW → 800 kg/h. The line m = a + bP: b = (800 − 500)/(40 − 20) = 15 kg/kWh; a = 500 − 15 × 20 = 200 kg/h (steam consumption at no load, supplying friction and windage).

steps.title: Predictions

steps.title: Refrigeration basics
steps.body:
**Refrigeration** removes heat from a low-temperature space and rejects it to a higher-temperature sink, requiring work (Clausius statement). **1 TR (tonne of refrigeration)** = heat to freeze 1 US ton (2000 lb) of ice at 0 °C in 24 h = **3.517 kW = 211 kJ/min = 12 000 BTU/h**.

**COP_ref = Q_L/W**; heat pump **COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_ref + 1**. Reversed Carnot (upper bound): **COP_ref,Carnot = T_L/(T_H − T_L)**, **COP_HP,Carnot = T_H/(T_H − T_L)**, temperatures in K.

**Relative COP** = actual/Carnot (0.4–0.7 typically). **EER** = capacity (BTU/h)/power (W); EER = 3.412 × COP.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** T_L = 263.15 K, T_H = 313.15 K: COP_Carnot = 263.15/50 = **5.263**; as heat pump 6.263.

**Ex 2.** 5 TR = 17.585 kW; actual COP 3 → W = 17.585/3 = **5.86 kW**; Carnot minimum W = 3.34 kW; relative COP = 0.57.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Carnot COP.
- Treating TR as power in the wrong unit (it is 3.517 kW).
- Confusing COP of refrigerator and heat pump (differ by exactly 1).
- Quoting COP > Carnot (violates the second law).

steps.title: Cycle
steps.body:
Reversed Joule (Bell–Coleman) cycle: 1→2 isentropic compression; 2→3 constant-pressure cooling in heat exchanger; 3→4 isentropic expansion in a turbine/expander; 4→1 constant-pressure heat absorption in cold space.

With r_p = p₂/p₁ and e = (γ−1)/γ: T₂ = T₁r_p^e, T₄ = T₃/r_p^e.
**Refrigeration effect** q_L = c_p(T₁ − T₄); **net work** W = c_p(T₂−T₁) − c_p(T₃−T₄); **COP = (T₁−T₄)/[(T₂−T₁)−(T₃−T₄)] = 1/(r_p^e − 1)**. COP is lower than the Carnot COP between the same extreme temperatures; higher r_p lowers COP. Used where air is the working fluid (aircraft).

steps.title: Why air cycles are rare on land
steps.body: COP ≈ 1–2 versus 3–5 for vapour compression, but air is safe, free and light — ideal for aircraft cabins.

steps.title: Why air cycles on aircraft
steps.body:
Light, no refrigerant leaks, uses engine-bleed or compressor air. **Simple system:** ram compression → compressor → heat exchanger (ram-air cooled) → turbine → cabin.

**Ram effect:** T₀₁ = T_a[1 + ((γ−1)/2)M²], p₀₁ = p_a[1 + ((γ−1)/2)M²]^(γ/(γ−1)). Isentropic efficiencies: η_c = (T₂s − T₁)/(T₂ − T₁); η_t = (T₃ − T₄)/(T₃ − T₄s). Cooling: Q = ṁ c_p (T_cabin − T₄). Variants: bootstrap, regenerative, reduced ambient — each adds heat exchanger/turbine stages to cool the bleed air further.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Ram: T₀₁ = 268(1 + 0.2×0.64) = **302.3 K**; p₀₁ = 0.65×1.128^3.5 = **0.991 bar**.

Compressor to 3.5 bar, η_c = 0.8: T₂s = 433.5 K → T₂ = **466.4 K**.

Cooled in the HX to 330 K; expand to cabin pressure 1.05 bar, η_t = 0.85: T₄s = 233.9 K → T₄ = **248.4 K**.

For a 10 kW cabin load held at 298 K: ṁ = Q/[c_p(298 − T₄)] = **0.200 kg/s**.

steps.title: Ice-plant energy
steps.body:
Heat to remove per kg: sensible cooling of water (c_pw = 4.187 kJ/kgK) from t₁ to 0 °C; latent heat of fusion **334 kJ/kg**; sub-cooling of ice (c_pi ≈ 2.1 kJ/kgK) to final temperature. **q = c_pw(t₁ − 0) + 334 + c_pi(0 − t_f)**.

Capacity = m q/(time). Add 10–20% for losses, and note that 1 TR (24 h) ≈ 1 US ton of ice → real plants need >1 TR per tonne because of sub-cooling and losses.

Cold-store loads: transmission, product (sensible + latent + respiration heat for fruit), infiltration, internal (lights, fans, people).

- Using 24 h vs operating hours (e.g. 20 h running) inconsistent.
- Mixing kJ and kW.

steps.title: Methods of refrigeration
steps.body:
1. **Vapour compression** — dominant: domestic fridges, AC, cold chain.
2. **Vapour absorption** — heat driven (waste heat, solar, gas): large chillers, caravans.
3. **Gas (air) cycles** — aircraft, cryogenic liquefaction.
4. **Steam-jet** — large chilled-water duty from process steam.
5. **Thermoelectric (Peltier)** — small coolers, CPUs, no moving parts.
6. **Vortex tube**, magnetic, thermoacoustic — niche.

**Applications:** domestic, commercial (display cases, cold rooms), industrial (ice plants, chemical, dairy), transport (reefer trucks, ships), air conditioning, food processing (freezing, freeze-drying), medical (vaccine cold chain at 2–8 °C).

scenes.text: A cold room needs 5 TR (17.585 kW). The plant uses R134a, evaporating at −10 °C and condensing at 40 °C.
Plot it on a p–h chart and calculate flow, power and COP.

steps.title: The four processes
steps.body:
1→2 **isentropic compression** (vapour, increases p and T); 2→3 **condensation** at constant p (desuperheat, condense, optional sub-cool); 3→4 **throttling** (isenthalpic, h₃ = h₄, flashes to a liquid–vapour mixture); 4→1 **evaporation** at constant p and T.

On the **p–h chart**: horizontal lines are isobars, the dome has saturated liquid (left) and vapour (right) lines; the cycle is a rectangle-like loop with evaporation/condensation horizontal, compression along a constant-s line, expansion a vertical line.

**q_L = h₁ − h₄**, **w = h₂ − h₁**, **q_H = h₂ − h₃**; COP = q_L/w; ṁ = Q_L/q_L; flash fraction x₄ = (h₄ − h_f,e)/h_fg,e.

steps.title: Solved example (rounded table values, kJ/kg)
steps.body:
h₁ = 392.5 (sat. vapour at −10 °C), h₂ = 422.0 (isentropic to 10.2 bar), h₃ = h₄ = 256.4 (sat. liquid at 40 °C).

q_L = 136.1; w = 29.5; **COP = 4.61**.

ṁ = 17.585/136.1 = **0.1292 kg/s**; compressor power = ṁw = **3.81 kW**; condenser duty = ṁ(h₂−h₃) = **21.40 kW** (= Q_L + W ✓).

steps.title: Reading a p–h chart
steps.body: Work and heat are horizontal distances — no need to integrate. A cycle that is 'wider' on the evaporator side relative to the compressor side has a higher COP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using h₄ ≠ h₃ (throttling is isenthalpic).
- Using the wrong enthalpy at state 1 (saturated vapour, not liquid).
- Mixing kJ/kg and kW without ṁ.
- Reading values from a chart with a different reference state in the same problem.

scenes.text: The same plant gains a liquid-suction heat exchanger and a larger condenser.

steps.title: Departures from the simple cycle
steps.body:
- **Sub-cooling** of liquid (below T_sat at condenser pressure) raises q_L at no extra compressor work → COP up.
- **Superheating** in the evaporator (useful if the heat comes from the cooled space) increases q_L but raises specific volume and work; net COP effect depends on the refrigerant. Superheat protects the compressor from liquid slugging.
- **Lower condensing pressure** (bigger condenser, cool water) reduces w; **higher evaporating pressure** raises q_L and reduces w. Each degree of lift costs ≈ 2–3% power.
- **Liquid–suction heat exchanger:** sub-cools liquid with cold suction vapour; helpful for R134a, harmful for NH₃ (very hot discharge).
- **Actual cycle:** pressure drops, compressor irreversibility (η_is), heat gain in suction line.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Add sub-cooling to 30 °C (h₃ = 241.7): q_L = 392.5−241.7 = 150.8; COP = 150.8/29.5 = **5.11** (vs 4.61), +10.8%.

With 10 K superheat (h₁ = 401.0, h₂ = 431.5) and sub-cooling: q_L = 159.3, w = 30.5, COP = **5.22**.

Actual compressor discharge 433 kJ/kg (not 422): η_is = 29.5/40.5 = **0.728**; real COP = **3.36**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Ignoring that a higher h₂ also means higher discharge temperature.
- Forgetting that isentropic efficiency lowers COP.

steps.title: Compressor performance
steps.body:
Types: **reciprocating** (hermetic, semi-hermetic), **rotary/scroll** (domestic, small AC), **screw** (industrial/commercial chillers), **centrifugal** (large chillers). **Volumetric efficiency** η_v = actual suction volume/swept volume; for a reciprocating machine with clearance factor c:

**η_v,clearance = 1 + c − c (p₂/p₁)^(1/n)** (n = polytropic exponent for re-expansion ≈ isentropic exponent: R134a ≈ 1.1–1.2, NH₃ ≈ 1.3).

Mass flow ṁ = η_v·V_swept·N/v₁. **Swept volume rate** V̇_s = ṁ v₁/η_v. **Shaft power** = ṁ w/(η_is η_mech η_motor). Higher pressure ratio → lower η_v, lower capacity; limits single-stage ratio to ~8–10 (R134a).

- Using liquid density for compressor flow.
- Ignoring that v₁ rises sharply at low evaporating temperature (capacity falls).

steps.title: Designation (ASHRAE 34)
steps.body:
For methane/ethane-based fluids R-xyz: z = number of F atoms; y = H atoms + 1; x = C atoms − 1 (omitted if 0); remaining bonds = Cl. R-22 → CHClF₂; R-12 → CCl₂F₂; R-134a → C₂H₂F₄ (a = isomer); R-717 = ammonia; R-744 = CO₂; R-290 = propane; R-600a = isobutane; R-718 = water; R-4xx blends (zeotropes), R-5xx azeotropes.

**Environmental indices:** ODP (ozone depletion potential, R-11 = 1), GWP (100-year global warming potential relative to CO₂). CFCs (R-12) and HCFCs (R-22) have ODP > 0 and were phased out under the **Montreal Protocol (1987)**; the **Kigali Amendment (2016)** phases down HFCs (high-GWP). Approximate GWP: R-134a ≈ 1300–1430; R-410A ≈ 2000; R-32 ≈ 675; R-290 ≈ 3; R-717 = 0; R-744 = 1. India has ratified Kigali and is shifting AC to lower-GWP options (R-32, R-290).

**Safety classes:** A1 (non-flammable, low toxicity), A2L (mildly flammable: R-32, R-1234yf), A3 (flammable: R-290, R-600a), B2L (toxic, mildly flammable: NH₃). **Selection:** thermodynamic properties (pressures, latent heat, COP), safety, compatibility with oil/materials, cost, environment.

steps.title: Decode and compare
steps.body:
R-22: x = 0, y = 1+1 = 2, z = 2 → C₁H₁F₂ + Cl = CHClF₂ ✓.

R-134a: 134 → C = 1+1 = 2, H = 3−1 = 2, F = 4 → C₂H₂F₄ ✓.

A hydrocarbon (R-290) has excellent COP and ~3 GWP but needs small charge limits because of flammability.

- Mixing blends into a system without checking glide.
- Confusing ODP with GWP (R-134a: ODP 0 but GWP high).
- Using non-approved flammable refrigerants in systems not designed for them.

steps.title: Why multistage
steps.body:
Single-stage compression is limited by (i) falling volumetric efficiency, (ii) very high discharge temperature (oil breakdown), (iii) high work. With **intercooling** between stages work falls. For ideal-gas behaviour and perfect intercooling to the initial temperature, work is minimum when the pressure ratios are equal:

**p_i = √(p_e p_c)** (geometric mean), N-stage: r = (p_c/p_e)^(1/N).

Polytropic work per kg (ideal gas): W = [n/(n−1)] R T₁[(p₂/p₁)^((n−1)/n) − 1] for each stage. In practice p_i is also tuned so that stage discharge temperatures and capacities match; ammonia plants often exceed ratio 8 and use two stages.

steps.title: Real fluids
steps.body: For refrigerants with superheated-vapour tables, find p_i by the geometric mean as a first guess, then optimise by trial on the p–h chart.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting intercooling reduces discharge temperature, not only work.
- Applying ideal-gas formula with the wrong n.

steps.title: Flash-chamber arrangement
steps.body:
LP compressor (1→2) discharges to the flash chamber/intercooler, where it is desuperheated by bubbling through saturated liquid at p_i. HP compressor (3→4) draws saturated vapour at p_i (state 3). Liquid from the condenser (state 5) is throttled to p_i (state 6, two-phase); saturated liquid (state 7, h_f at p_i) feeds the evaporator via a second throttle (h₈ = h₇).

Mass balance: LP flow ṁ₁ (evaporator), HP flow ṁ₃. Energy balance on the intercooler: **ṁ₃ h₃ + ṁ₁ h₇ = ṁ₃ h₆ + ṁ₁ h₂ → ṁ₃/ṁ₁ = (h₂ − h₇)/(h₃ − h₆)**.

Q_e = ṁ₁(h₁ − h₇); W = ṁ₁(h₂ − h₁) + ṁ₃(h₄ − h₃); COP = Q_e/W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ṁ₁ in the HP term.
- Forgetting the flash vapour in the HP flow.
- Taking h₇ = h₅ (it is saturated liquid at p_i).

steps.title: One compressor, two temperatures
steps.body:
The warmer evaporator (E₁) runs at higher pressure; a **back-pressure (evaporator-pressure-regulating) valve** throttles its vapour to the common suction pressure, then the two vapour streams mix before the compressor. Individual liquid flows: ṁ_i = Q_i/(h_g,i − h_f).

Suction state from mixing: h_mix = Σṁ_i h_i/Σṁ_i (the throttled stream has the same enthalpy as its saturated vapour state). Compressor work W = ṁ_total(h₂ − h_mix). **COP = ΣQ_i/W**. Alternative: separate compressors or compound systems — more efficient (E₁ is not compressed from −10 °C).

steps.body: The 5 °C evaporator vapour is throttled down to −10 °C pressure — an irreversibility. Separate suction groups avoid it.

steps.title: Cascade
steps.body:
Used below ≈ −40 °C where a single refrigerant would have too low suction pressure (huge v₁) or freeze. **Low-temperature (LT) circuit** (e.g. R-23/R-508B/R-170, CO₂ in transcritical-subcritical) evaporates at the cold temperature and condenses at an intermediate temperature; the **cascade condenser/evaporator** transfers its condenser heat to the **high-temperature (HT) circuit** (e.g. R-134a, NH₃, propane) which evaporates there and condenses to ambient.

Balance: **ṁ_L(h₂ − h₃)_L = ṁ_H(h₅ − h₈)_H**. Total work = W_L + W_H; **COP = Q_L/(W_L+W_H)**. A temperature difference of 5–10 K is needed in the cascade exchanger, and an expansion tank accommodates LT refrigerant expansion when the plant is off.

steps.title: Where used
steps.body: Biomedical −80 °C freezers, liquefaction of gases, freeze-drying, and CO₂/NH₃ supermarket systems.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting cascade ΔT to zero (no heat flow).
- Adding capacities instead of work.
- Using the HT refrigerant properties for the LT circuit.

lessons.title: Lab: Heat pumps and comparison with electric heating

scenes.text: A heat pump delivers 3 kW of heating to a room using COP = 4.
How much electricity does that save versus a resistance heater?

steps.title: Heat pump
steps.body:
A heat pump is a refrigerator whose useful effect is Q_H (rejected heat). **COP_HP = Q_H/W = 1 + COP_ref**. Ideal: T_H/(T_H − T_L). Sources: air, ground (geothermal, stable T), water. Reversible split-ACs (inverter) switch between heating and cooling via a **four-way reversing valve**. **Seasonal performance:** SCOP/HSPF; heating COP falls when outdoor air is colder and defrosting is needed.

Compared with resistance heating (COP = 1): COP 3–4 uses 25–33% of the electricity. In India, reversible ACs are used in northern winters and for water heating (heat-pump water heaters).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Q_H = 3 kW, COP = 4 → W = **0.75 kW**; electric heater needs 3 kW → saves 2.25 kW (75%).

Carnot limit for T_H = 313.15 K, T_L = 273.15 K: COP = **7.83**; the real 4.0 is 51% of Carnot.

Running 8 h/day, 90 days at ₹8/kWh: electricity saved = 2.25×8×90 = 1620 kWh = **₹12,960**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using COP_ref for heating questions.
- Using °C in Carnot.
- Ignoring the capacity drop at low outdoor temperature.

lessons.title: Lab: Principle of vapour absorption refrigeration

scenes.text: A hospital has waste heat from a gas engine and wants chilled water without a big electric compressor.
An absorber, pump and generator replace the compressor.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Absorption replaces the mechanical compressor by a **thermal compressor**: the absorber dissolves refrigerant vapour in a liquid absorbent (releasing heat), a small **solution pump** raises its pressure (liquid pumping needs little work), the **generator** boils the refrigerant out using heat at T_g, the condenser, expansion valve and evaporator work as in the vapour compression system.

**Pairs:** NH₃–H₂O (NH₃ refrigerant; needs rectifier/analyser because water also vaporises; can go below 0 °C), **LiBr–H₂O** (water refrigerant; evaporator > ~4 °C; vacuum; crystallisation at high concentration).

**Energy balance:** Q_g + Q_e + W_pump = Q_c + Q_a. **COP = Q_e/Q_g** (pump work neglected).

**Ideal COP** (three reservoirs, reversible): **COP_max = [(T_g − T_a)/T_g]·[T_e/(T_a − T_e)]** — a Carnot engine driving a Carnot refrigerator.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Absorption chillers run on waste heat, steam, solar thermal or natural gas — common in hotels, hospitals and textile units where heat is cheaper than electricity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling absorption 'no energy'.
- Using COP > 1 for absorption in single effect.
- Using °C in the ideal COP formula.

lessons.title: Lab: LiBr–water chillers: single and double effect

scenes.text: A hotel selects a 100 TR LiBr chiller. Heat input and cooling-water rejection must be known.
Double-effect machines recover heat internally.

steps.title: LiBr–H₂O chiller
steps.body:
Components: evaporator (water at ~4–7 mm Hg abs, 5–7 °C), absorber (LiBr solution absorbs vapour; cooled by tower water), solution pump, **solution heat exchanger** (recovers heat from hot strong solution to cool weak solution), generator (hot water/steam/direct fired), condenser. Concentrations typically ≈ 55% weak → ≈ 60% strong LiBr by mass; **circulation ratio f = x_s/(x_s − x_w)** kg weak solution per kg refrigerant.

**Double effect:** vapour from a high-pressure generator (heated by steam/gas) drives a second generator, reusing latent heat: COP ≈ 1.1–1.4 versus 0.65–0.8 single. Needs higher temperatures (~150–170 °C).

**Heat rejection:** Q_c + Q_a = Q_e + Q_g, so the cooling tower is larger than for an electric chiller.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Q_e = 100 TR = **351.7 kW**. Single effect COP 0.7: Q_g = 502.4 kW; heat rejected = Q_e + Q_g = **854.1 kW** (an electric chiller at COP 5 rejects only 422 kW).

Double effect COP 1.2: Q_g = **293.1 kW** — 42% less heat.

Circulation ratio for x_w = 0.55, x_s = 0.60: f = 0.60/0.05 = **12** kg solution per kg water vapour.

steps.title: Crystallisation
steps.body: Strong solution that cools below its saturation line crystallises and blocks the heat exchanger — controls dilute the solution on shutdown.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the large heat-rejection load.
- Using the NH₃–H₂O rectifier for LiBr (not needed — LiBr is non-volatile).
- Setting evaporator temperature below ~4 °C in a water-refrigerant machine.

lessons.title: Lab: NH₃–water, Electrolux and domestic absorption

scenes.text: A camper's fridge has no compressor and no moving parts, running on gas or a heater.
It uses three fluids: NH₃, H₂O, H₂.

steps.title: NH₃–H₂O system
steps.body:
Both components are volatile: vapour leaving the generator carries water, so an **analyser and rectifier** purify it (to ~99% NH₃). Absorber at low pressure; refrigerant NH₃ evaporates at −30 to +5 °C. Pressure losses are large, so ejectors/pumps are used in large plants.

**Electrolux (three-fluid) refrigerator:** total pressure is uniform; **hydrogen** gas in the evaporator lowers NH₃ partial pressure so it evaporates at low temperature without an expansion valve; a **bubble (percolator) pump** lifts weak solution using the generator's heat. No moving parts → silent; COP ≈ 0.2–0.3. Ideal for hotel minibars, RVs and off-grid health clinics.

**Compare** with vapour compression: higher cost/lower COP but no noise or electricity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A minibar absorbs 30 W of heat; with COP 0.25 the generator needs 30/0.25 = **120 W** of heat. A compressor fridge at COP 2.5 would need 12 W of electricity — but the absorption unit can run on a gas flame or a 120 W heater.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body: Low-vibration cooling is also valuable in laboratories and sleeping quarters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the Electrolux has a mechanical pump.
- Forgetting rectifier is required for NH₃–water.
- Expecting high COP.

lessons.title: Lab: Steam-jet, thermoelectric and vortex-tube cooling

scenes.text: Three very different devices: an ejector chiller, a Peltier cooler and a vortex tube.
Each has a niche.

steps.title: Steam-jet refrigeration
steps.body:
Motive steam passes through a nozzle, entrains vapour from a flash chamber (water boils at ~5–10 °C under 0.9–1.2 kPa), diffuses, and is condensed. Water is the refrigerant — chilled water at 4–10 °C for process/AC where cheap steam exists. Flash fraction x = c_p ΔT/h_fg. Very low COP (0.2–0.3 per steam), large vacuum equipment.

**Thermoelectric (Peltier):** current through p–n junctions pumps heat. With Seebeck coefficient α, resistance R, thermal conductance K: **Q_c = αIT_c − ½I²R − K ΔT**; **W = I²R + αIΔT**; **COP = Q_c/W**; optimum current for max Q_c at ΔT=0 is I = αT_c/R.

**Vortex tube:** compressed air entering tangentially splits into a cold stream (near axis) and hot stream (periphery) — no moving parts; low efficiency (COP ≈ 0.1–0.2), used for spot cooling.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Steam jet:** 100 kW chilled water duty, ΔT = 5 K: ṁ_w = 100/(4.187×5) = 4.78 kg/s; flash fraction = 4.187×5/2485 = 0.0084 → **0.040 kg/s** vapour must be entrained.

**Peltier module:** α = 0.05 V/K, R = 2 Ω, K = 0.5 W/K, I = 3 A, T_c = 275 K, T_h = 300 K: Q_c = 41.25 − 9.0 − 12.5 = **19.75 W**; W = 18 + 3.75 = **21.75 W**; COP = **0.91**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting Joule heating ½I²R is shared equally.
- Using °C in the Seebeck formula.
- Expecting steam jets to work for 0 °C or below (water would freeze).

scenes.text: A consultant must recommend a cooling technology for five sites.

steps.title: Selection criteria
steps.body:
Energy source (electricity vs heat), temperature level, capacity, noise/vibration, reliability/maintenance, capital vs running cost, refrigerant safety (flammability/toxicity), environmental regulations. Rules of thumb: > −35 °C one or two-stage vapour compression; below −40 °C cascade; waste heat available → absorption; very small silent → Peltier/absorption; aircraft → air cycle; process steam & chilled water → steam-jet.

Lifecycle cost: electricity ≈ 70–80% of life cost of a compressor chiller in India's hot climate; inverter drives and good heat-rejection design pay back quickly.

steps.title: Quick matching
steps.body: Dairy chilling at 4 °C with grid power → screw chiller (vapour compression); pharmaceutical −80 °C freezer → cascade; textile mill with surplus 150 °C steam → double-effect LiBr; remote health-post vaccine fridge with no grid → gas/solar absorption or solar-direct-drive compressor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Selecting only on first cost.
- Ignoring local service availability.
- Overlooking safety codes for NH₃ and flammables.

lessons.title: Lab: Moist-air properties — W, φ, h, v and dew point

scenes.text: Outside air is 30 °C and 60% relative humidity.
What is the humidity ratio, enthalpy and dew point?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Moist air = dry air + water vapour (Dalton: P = p_a + p_v). **Relative humidity φ = p_v/p_g** (p_g = saturation pressure at the dry-bulb temperature). **Humidity ratio ω = 0.622 p_v/(P − p_v)** (kg vapour/kg dry air). **Degree of saturation μ = ω/ω_s**. **Dew-point temperature** = saturation temperature at p_v. **Enthalpy per kg dry air: h = 1.005 t + ω(2501 + 1.88 t)** kJ/kg_da. **Specific volume** v = R_a T/(P − p_v) = 0.287 T/(P − p_v) m³/kg_da. Saturation pressures: 20 °C 2.339 kPa, 25 °C 3.170, 30 °C 4.247, 35 °C 5.629, 40 °C 7.385 kPa.

The **psychrometric chart** plots ω vs t with lines of φ, h, wet-bulb and v.

steps.title: Quick rules
steps.body: Sensible heat: 1.005 kJ/kg·K (≈1.02 with vapour). Latent heat: 2501 kJ/kg. On the chart, dew point is found by moving horizontally (constant ω) to the saturation curve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total pressure as p_v.
- ω in g/kg vs kg/kg.
- Reading RH as 'amount of water'.
- Using ρ = P/RT without subtracting p_v.

lessons.title: Lab: Wet-bulb, adiabatic saturation and psychrometer

scenes.text: A sling psychrometer reads dry bulb 30 °C and wet bulb 22 °C.

steps.title: Adiabatic saturation and WBT
steps.body:
**Adiabatic saturation temperature t*:** air flowing over water in an insulated duct, leaves saturated at t*. Energy balance gives:

**ω = [(2501 − 2.381 t*) ω* − 1.005 (t − t*)]/(2501 + 1.805 t − 4.186 t*)**, where ω* is the saturation humidity ratio at t*.

The **thermodynamic wet-bulb** equals t* by definition; for air–water the measured wet-bulb (ventilated > 3–5 m/s) is within ~0.2 K of t* because Lewis number ≈ 0.9–1. Then use chart or the formula for ω and φ. **Dew point ≤ wet-bulb ≤ dry-bulb**, all equal at saturation.

steps.title: Evaporative cooler limit
steps.body: A direct evaporative cooler can approach the wet-bulb temperature — in dry Rajasthan summers (e.g. t = 42, t_wb = 24) it can supply ~28 °C air cheaply; in humid Mumbai monsoon it barely works.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using wet-bulb as dew point.
- Not ventilating the wet-bulb sock (reads high).
- Using φ and ω interchangeably.

lessons.title: Lab: Psychrometric processes — heating, cooling, humidifying, mixing

scenes.text: A plant mixes 3 kg/s of return air (20 °C, ω = 0.008) with 1 kg/s of fresh air (35 °C, ω = 0.018).
What are the mixed state and the coil inlet?

steps.title: Basic processes
steps.body:
- **Sensible heating/cooling:** ω constant; Q = ṁ_a(1.005+1.88ω)Δt.
- **Humidification** (steam or water spray): ω increases; steam raises h slightly and t little; adiabatic spray moves along constant-h (wet-bulb) line.
- **Cooling & dehumidification:** air touches a coil below its dew point; Q_total = ṁ_a(h₁ − h₂) − ṁ_a(ω₁ − ω₂)h_f; sensible part Q_s = ṁ_a c_pm (t₁ − t₂); latent Q_L = Q_total − Q_s; **SHF = Q_s/Q_total**.
- **Chemical dehumidification:** ω falls, t rises (constant h approx).
- **Mixing of two streams:** mass-weighted mixing of ω and h (the mixed state lies on the straight line joining the two on the chart); temperature is approximately weighted too: t₃ ≈ (ṁ₁t₁ + ṁ₂t₂)/(ṁ₁ + ṁ₂).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing on volumetric (not mass) basis.
- Forgetting the condensate enthalpy term.
- Treating cooling as sensible-only after hitting the dew point.

lessons.title: Lab: Cooling coil, apparatus dew point and bypass factor

scenes.text: A coil at 7 °C surface cools humid air; some air touches the coil, some bypasses.
The coil leaving state lies on a line to the ADP.

steps.title: Coil model
steps.body:
Air leaving a coil is a mix of fully conditioned air (at the **apparatus dew point, ADP** ≈ coil surface temperature) and unaffected bypass air. **Bypass factor BF = (t₂ − t_ADP)/(t₁ − t_ADP)**; **contact factor CF = 1 − BF**. The process line 1→2 extends to the saturation curve at ADP. Lower BF (more rows, slower air, closer fin spacing) means colder, drier air.

Sensible-only: ω constant if coil surface above dew point. Required ADP for a given room condition follows from the **effective sensible heat factor** (ESHF): draw ESHF line from room state, intersect saturation curve at ADP.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Coil inlet 30 °C, ADP 10 °C, outlet 14 °C: BF = (14−10)/(30−10) = **0.20**; CF = **0.80**.

Outlet ω by the same ratio: ω₂ = ω_ADP + BF(ω₁ − ω_ADP) — with ω_ADP = 0.00766 (sat. at 10 °C) and ω₁ = 0.01601: ω₂ = **0.00933**.

If the coil has 4 rows with BF = 0.35 and two more rows are added, BF becomes ≈ 0.35² ≈ 0.12 (each row bypasses equal fraction).

steps.title: Selecting the coil
steps.body: A deeper coil or lower face velocity reduces BF but increases air-side pressure drop — pick economically.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up ADP with outlet temperature.
- Setting BF = 0 (ideal, impossible).
- Ignoring coil entering-wet-bulb effect on capacity.

scenes.text: A seminar hall holds 50 people. CO₂ climbs and attendees complain of stuffiness.
How much outdoor air keeps CO₂ within a small rise?

steps.title: Comfort
steps.body:
Comfort depends on air temperature, mean radiant temperature, relative humidity, air speed, clothing (clo) and activity (met). **Fanger PMV/PPD** model; **ASHRAE 55** comfort zone ≈ 23–26 °C operative temperature, 30–60% RH in still air. Indian adaptive-comfort (NBC 2016 / IMAC) allows wider ranges in naturally ventilated buildings. Air speeds 0.2–0.5 m/s are fine; > 0.8 m/s causes draught.

**Ventilation:** need fresh air to dilute CO₂, odours and pollutants. Steady CO₂ balance: **C_in − C_out = G/Q** where G = generation (m³/s) and Q = outdoor air (m³/s). A person generates ≈ 0.005 L/s of CO₂ (sedentary). Typical office ventilation: 7–10 L/s per person (use the local code table). Air changes per hour ACH = 3600 Q/V.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
G per person = 0.005 L/s; Q = 8 L/s per person: ΔC = 0.005/8 = 0.000625 = **625 ppm** above outdoor (≈ 420 ppm) → ~1045 ppm; CO₂ stays below ~1000 ppm.

Hall of 50 people: Q = 50×8 = 400 L/s = 0.4 m³/s; volume 600 m³ → ACH = 3600×0.4/600 = **2.4**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating CO₂ ppm as toxic (it is an indicator of ventilation).
- Cooling to very low temperatures — draughts and humidity matter too.
- Using only RH as comfort.

lessons.title: Lab: Cooling-load estimation — sensible and latent components

scenes.text: A 150 m² office, 20 occupants, 36 °C outside and 24 °C inside, needs a cooling-load estimate.
Sum envelope, solar, people, lights, equipment and infiltration.

steps.title: Load components
steps.body:
**External:** wall/roof conduction Q = U A ΔT_eq (CLTD method uses cooling-load temperature difference to account for storage); **solar gain through glass** Q = A·SHGC·G (shading coefficient SC method); infiltration/ventilation (sensible 1.2·1.005·V̇ Δt kW and latent 1.2·V̇·Δω·2500 kW, V̇ in m³/s). **Internal:** people (≈ 75 W sensible + 55 W latent seated, light work), lights (W/m² × area), equipment (computers ≈ 100–150 W each), motors. **Safety factor** 5–10%.

**Sensible vs latent:** sensible raises dry-bulb, latent changes ω. **Room sensible heat factor RSHF = RSH/(RSH + RLH)**. Total load in TR = kW/3.517. Software (HAP, Carrier, eQUEST) or ISHRAE/ASHRAE tables are used for final design.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Wall 40 m², U = 0.45 → 0.22 kW; glass 10 m²: conduction (U = 2.8) 0.34 kW + solar (SHGC 0.5, 450 W/m²) 2.25 kW; people sensible 1.50; lights 3.0; equipment 2.0; infiltration (0.05 m³/s) 0.72.

**RSH = 10.03 kW**.

Latent: people 1.10 + infiltration (Δω = 0.010) 1.50 = **RLH = 2.60 kW**.

Total = **12.63 kW = 3.59 TR** (add 10% → 3.9 TR); RSHF = 0.79.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding latent loads to sensible ones in the wrong place (affects SHF and coil ADP).
- Using peak outdoor temperature for all components regardless of time.
- Counting solar gain through opaque walls twice.
- Forgetting people and equipment latent loads.

lessons.title: Lab: Room sensible heat factor and supply-air quantity

story.title: How much air do we supply?

scenes.text: A room has 30 kW sensible and 10 kW latent load. Supply air arrives at 13 °C; room is 24 °C.
Find airflow in m³/s and the room ratio line.

steps.title: Supply air
steps.body: **RSHF = RSH/(RSH + RLH)**; the **room ratio line** (slope fixed by RSHF) passes through the room state. Supply state must lie on this line. **Supply air mass flow** (dry air) from the sensible balance: **ṁ_a = RSH/[c_pm (t_r − t_s)]** with c_pm = 1.005 + 1.88ω ≈ 1.02 kJ/kg·K. Latent balance: ṁ_a(ω_r − ω_s) h_fg = RLH ⇒ ω_s = ω_r − RLH/(ṁ_a·2501). Volume flow V̇ = ṁ_a v. Supply ΔT of 8–11 K is typical (lower than 8 K wastes fan power, more than 12 K risks draught and condensation).

steps.title: Sizing check
steps.body: Airflow per TR ≈ 100–120 cfm (≈ 0.05–0.06 m³/s) for typical comfort cooling with SHF 0.7–0.8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total load for airflow (use sensible).
- Using supply ΔT from the unit's rated value rather than the actual.
- Mixing volume and mass flows.

lessons.title: Lab: Coil load with fresh air and the complete design

scenes.text: The room is supplied at 13 °C, ω = 0.0080 g/kg. 30% fresh air at 34 °C, ω = 0.0185 mixes with return air before the coil.

steps.title: Complete design procedure
steps.body:
1. Estimate RSH, RLH → RSHF. 2. Choose room state (24 °C, 50%). 3. Draw room ratio line; pick supply state (ΔT 8–11 K). 4. Compute ṁ_a. 5. Add fresh air: mix state (mass-weighted). 6. Coil inlet = mix state, outlet = supply state (if no reheat). 7. **Coil load = ṁ_a(h_mix − h_s) − ṁ_a(ω_mix − ω_s)h_f**. 8. Add fan heat (≈ 1–2 K rise) and duct gains. Fresh-air load is often 20–30% of total in Indian conditions.

**Effective RSHF** accounts for bypassed outdoor air; **ESHF = (RSH + OASH)/(RSH + RLH + OASH + OALH)** and defines ADP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using room state at coil inlet when fresh air is mixed.
- Forgetting that the fresh-air latent load can exceed the room latent load.
- Ignoring fan and duct heat gains.

lessons.title: Lab: Duct design — equal-friction and fan power

scenes.text: A branch carries 2 m³/s at 6 m/s. Fan static pressure is 400 Pa.
Find duct size and fan power.

steps.title: Air distribution
steps.body:
**Continuity:** A = V̇/v. **Round duct** D = √(4A/π). **Equivalent diameter of a rectangular duct** (same friction): D_e = 1.3 (ab)^0.625/(a + b)^0.25. **Velocity pressure** p_v = ½ρv². **Total pressure** = static + velocity. Friction loss (Darcy) Δp = f (L/D) ½ρv².

**Methods:** *equal friction* (0.8–1.2 Pa/m, simplest), *velocity reduction*, *static regain* (VAV/high velocity). Typical velocities: main ducts 6–9 m/s, branches 3–5 m/s, grilles < 2.5 m/s; keep noise low (NC 30–40).

**Fan power** P = V̇ Δp/η_fan; fan laws: Q ∝ N, Δp ∝ N², P ∝ N³. Add fittings via equivalent length or loss coefficients C (Δp = C p_v).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
A = 2/6 = 0.333 m² → D = **651 mm**.

Rectangular 600×400: D_e = 1.3×(0.24)^0.625/(1.0)^0.25 = **533 mm** — the circular duct with the same friction loss.

Velocity pressure at 6 m/s = ½×1.2×36 = **21.6 Pa**. Fan power = 2×400/0.6 = **1333 W** (electrical power = / motor η).

steps.title: Fan laws
steps.body: Reducing fan speed by 20% cuts power to 0.8³ = 51% of full — why VAV and VFDs save energy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using duct area for velocity pressure in the wrong units.
- Sizing grilles at > 3 m/s (noise).
- Ignoring dirty-filter pressure drop in fan selection.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — complete AC design for a small clinic

scenes.text: A 120 m² clinic in Pune: 36 °C/24 °C wet-bulb ≈ 22 °C design, indoor 24 °C, 50%. Loads: RSH 18 kW, RLH 4 kW, fresh air 0.25 m³/s.
Complete the design steps in order and check one numerical result.

steps.title: Capstone
steps.body: You must select the capacity, airflow, coil state and fan. Use RSHF = 18/22 = 0.82. Take supply ΔT = 10 K (t_s = 14 °C), c_pm = 1.02: ṁ_a = 18/(1.02×10) = 1.765 kg/s → V̇ = 1.47 m³/s. Fresh air 0.25 m³/s ≈ 0.30 kg/s ≈ 17% of supply. Fresh-air load (sensible + latent, outdoor 36 °C/ω 0.0205 vs room 24 °C/ω 0.0093) ≈ 0.30×(h_oa − h_r) where h_oa = 1.005×36 + 0.0205×(2501+67.7) = 88.8; h_r = 47.6 → 12.4 kW. Coil ≈ 22 + 12.4 + fan heat ≈ 36 kW ≈ 10 TR.

steps.title: System families
steps.body:
- **Window / split (ductless):** 0.8–3 TR rooms; split = indoor + outdoor unit; inverter types modulate compressor speed.
- **Ducted split / packaged (rooftop):** 3–50 TR; air distributed by ducts.
- **VRF/VRV:** one outdoor unit serves many indoor units via refrigerant piping; zone control, heat recovery options; refrigerant-charge limits per room (safety).
- **Central chilled water:** screw/centrifugal chillers + AHUs/FCUs; > 100 TR; best efficiency, thermal storage possible.
- **All-air (VAV, CAV), air-water (FCU + DOAS), all-water.**
- **Evaporative cooling:** hot-dry climates; **radiant/chilled-beam** + dedicated outdoor air (DOAS).
- **District cooling** for campuses/cities (e.g., large IT parks).

steps.title: Selection thinking
steps.body: A 10-room hotel wing with zones that have different occupancy and an existing 100 TR load → VRF or a chilled-water FCU system. A single 15 m² server room → dedicated precision split with N+1 redundancy. A 1000 TR IT park → central chillers with variable primary flow and thermal storage.

lessons.title: Lab: Cooling towers — range, approach and make-up water

scenes.text: A 500-TR chiller rejects heat to a cooling tower: 50 kg/s water, 37 °C in, 31 °C out, wet-bulb 27 °C.

steps.title: Cooling-tower performance
steps.body:
Types: natural draught (hyperbolic, power stations), mechanical induced/forced draught, counterflow vs crossflow, closed-circuit. **Range = T_in − T_out**; **Approach = T_out − T_wb** (cannot be < 0); **Effectiveness = Range/(Range + Approach)**. Heat rejected Q = ṁ_w c_w Range. **Evaporation loss** E ≈ Q/h_fg ≈ 0.0017 × ṁ_w × Range kg/s (≈ 1% of flow per 6 K range). **Cycles of concentration COC = TDS_circulating/TDS_makeup**; blowdown B = E/(COC − 1); drift loss small (0.001–0.005%). **Make-up M = E + B + D.**

Common problems: scaling, biofouling and Legionella (water treatment and biocide dosing, maintenance schedules required).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using dry-bulb for approach.
- Forgetting blowdown in make-up water.
- Skipping water treatment (Legionella risk).

steps.title: Capacity control
steps.body:
Methods: on/off cycling (small), cylinder unloading, hot-gas bypass (wastes energy), suction throttling, slide-valve (screw), inlet guide vanes (centrifugal), **variable-speed drives (VFD/inverter)** — best at part load. Reciprocating clearance volumetric efficiency: η_v = 1 + c − c(p₂/p₁)^(1/n).

**Chiller performance:** kW/TR (full-load 0.55–0.7 for water-cooled screw/centrifugal; lower is better). **IPLV/NPLV** weights 100/75/50/25% load; Indian practice uses ISEER (for room ACs), IPLV for chillers. Pump & fan power ∝ speed³ with VFD.

steps.title: Why VFD
steps.body: Compressor/fan/pump cube-law savings; most hours run below 60% load.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using hot-gas bypass as the primary control.
- Judging chillers by full-load kW/TR only.
- Forgetting pumps and tower fans in plant kW/TR.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.body:
**COP = Q/W** (dimensionless). **EER = Btu/h per W** = 3.412 × COP (BEE's older EER). **ISEER** (Indian Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio) weights temperature bins across India's climate, used for BEE star labels on room ACs — higher ISEER, more stars. **kW/TR** for chillers.

Running cost = (kW × hours × tariff). Standby power, inverter modulation, refrigerant (R-32/R-290) and heat-exchanger area drive efficiency. Rated capacity is at standard conditions (35 °C outdoor, 27 °C/19 °C indoor wb).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
1.5 TR = 5.28 kW capacity, input 1.5 kW: COP = **3.52**; EER = 12.0 Btu/Wh.

Running 8 h/day for 240 days: 1.5×8×240 = **2880 kWh** → at ₹8/kWh = **₹23,040** per year. A unit at COP 4.2 would use 1.26 kW: saving ≈ ₹3,747/year.

steps.title: Diagnostic method
steps.body: Check **airflow** (filters, coil, fan), **charge** (superheat/sub-cooling), **electrical** (voltage, capacitor, contactor), **controls** (thermostat set-point/mode), and **heat load** (door open, extra occupants). Safety: switch off, discharge capacitors, wear gloves/goggles, recover (not vent) refrigerant, follow lock-out/tag-out. Gauges: low-side pressure low + high superheat → undercharge or restriction; high head + high sub-cooling → overcharge or dirty condenser.

steps.title: Typical readings (R-32 split)
steps.body: Suction 6.2 bar (sat ≈ 4 °C), line 24 °C → superheat 20 K (high); liquid 41 °C, condensing sat 44 °C → sub-cooling 3 K (low). Diagnosis: **undercharge/leak**. Fix: find leak (nitrogen pressure test + soap/electronic detector), repair, evacuate to < 500 micron, weigh in correct charge.

steps.title: Do not

- Top-up without leak repair (illegal/pollution).
- Use the wrong refrigerant.
- Work on live equipment.

steps.title: Cycles & units
steps.body:
- 1 TR = 3.517 kW; COP = Q_L/W; COP_HP = COP_ref + 1; Carnot T_L/(T_H − T_L).
- Bell–Coleman: T₂ = T₁ r^((γ−1)/γ); COP = 1/(r^((γ−1)/γ) − 1).

steps.title: Aim, apparatus and theory
steps.body:
**Aim:** determine actual COP and relative COP of a VCR test rig. **Apparatus:** hermetic compressor, air-cooled condenser, capillary tube/TXV, evaporator coil in a water bath, pressure gauges (LP/HP), RTDs, energy meter, stopwatch, 10 kg water.

steps.title: Calculation

The low value is typical for a small hermetic unit: motor, compressor and heat-gain losses, a poorly insulated water bath, and pressure drops.

- Keep the condenser airflow clear.

steps.title: Power–torque relation
steps.body:
T = 60·P/(2πN). In handy units **T (N·mm) = 9.55×10⁶ · P(kW) / N(rpm)**.

For a solid round shaft in pure torsion: **τ = 16T/(πd³)**, so d = (16T/(πτ))^(1/3). Hollow shaft with k = d_i/d_o: τ = 16T/(πd_o³(1−k⁴)).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:

Allowable τ = 40 MPa → d³ = 16T/(πτ) → **d = 31.2 mm**, round up to the standard **35 mm**.

- Using rpm directly as rad/s.
